opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've thought about a lot, because a lot of my work, going back to the early state space model papers and even before that, has really been about structured matrices in one form or another.

The basic tension is this: a fully dense, unstructured matrix is the most expressive linear map you can have, but it's expensive. You pay quadratic cost in parameters and in compute for matrix-vector multiplication. Structured matrices, like low-rank, sparse, Toeplitz, Fourier-like, butterfly, or the semiseparable matrices that show up in SSMs, give you much faster algorithms, often near-linear time, and far fewer parameters. The question is always what you give up in expressivity, and whether that matters for the problem.

I think the naive framing is "structure equals restriction, so it's a compromise." That's only half the story. The right structure is also an inductive bias. Convolutions are the classic example: a convolution is a highly structured matrix, and that structure is exactly why CNNs work so well on images. You're not just saving compute, you're encoding something true about the data, like translation equivariance. So with a good structure you get efficiency and better generalization or sample efficiency together.

Where it gets tricky is that structure has a cost beyond expressivity, and that's hardware. Some structured matrices have great asymptotic complexity but terrible constant factors on GPUs, because GPUs are built to do dense matrix multiplies extremely well. An FFT-based method might be O(n log n) on paper and still lose to a well-tuned dense matmul at practical sizes. A lot of the engineering in this area, including what we did with Mamba and later with state space duality, is about finding structures that are both theoretically efficient and expressible in hardware-friendly primitives, like block decompositions where most of the work is still small dense matmuls.

So my mental model has three axes. First, expressivity: can this family represent the transformations you actually need? Second, algorithmic efficiency: is there a fast algorithm, and how does it scale with sequence length or dimension? Third, hardware efficiency: does it map well onto the accelerators we have? A good structured matrix family balances all three, and often the most interesting research comes from realizing that two seemingly different structures, say a recurrence and a form of masked attention, are actually the same matrix viewed differently. That gives you the freedom to choose whichever computational form suits the situation.

And then, more philosophically, I think it comes down to compression. Intelligence, in some sense, is about compressing information efficiently. Structured matrices are one principled way to build that compression into the architecture, rather than hoping a giant dense model learns it all on its own.

r001.rationale: It says a fully dense, unstructured matrix is the most expressive linear map and frames structured matrices as giving up some expressivity.

r002.rationale: It describes structure as an inductive bias and explains that convolutional structure encodes translation equivariance, which suits image problems.

r003.rationale: It contrasts dense matrix-vector multiplication’s quadratic cost with structured matrices’ faster algorithms, often near-linear time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because a big chunk of my work going back to my PhD was really about structured matrices. And the way I think about it is that it's fundamentally a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency, and the interesting question is whether you can find structure that gets you most of the efficiency without giving up the expressivity you actually need.

So just to back up, a dense matrix is the most general thing. You've got n squared parameters, it can represent any linear map, and it costs n squared compute to apply. That's your baseline, that's what a standard linear layer is. A structured matrix is anything where you impose some constraint on the form of the matrix so that it has fewer parameters and, more importantly, a faster algorithm for matrix-vector multiplication. Classic examples would be things like low-rank matrices, sparse matrices, Toeplitz or circulant matrices, Fourier-type transforms, and so on. Many of these have multiplication algorithms that are n log n or even linear instead of quadratic.

Now, the naive view is that you're just trading off accuracy for speed, you're restricting the function class so it has to be worse. And that's true in a vacuum. But the thing I found really compelling, and this was the thesis of a lot of my early work, was that in deep learning you often don't actually want a fully general matrix. The dense matrix is a kind of default that we use because it's easy and because the hardware is good at it, not because we've thought carefully about what the right inductive bias is. So the question becomes, can you find a class of structured matrices that is matched to the problem? Like, a convolution is a structured matrix, it's a Toeplitz matrix, and nobody thinks of a convolution as a limitation. It's the thing that made computer vision work. The structure is the inductive bias.

So the way I frame it now is less "structured versus dense" and more, what is the structure encoding, and does that match the data. And the places where this has really paid off for me are in sequence modeling. The state space models, S4 and then Mamba, those are really structured matrices at their core. The whole recurrence can be written as a particular structured matrix acting on the sequence, and the reason you get linear time scaling instead of quadratic like attention is exactly because of that structure. And the reason it doesn't completely fall apart on long-range dependencies is because we were careful about which structure we picked, that HiPPO initialization and so on. So that's a case where the structure is doing a lot of work for you rather than fighting you.

The other side of the trade-off, and I think this is the part people underestimate, is the hardware side. There's a theoretical efficiency and then there's a practical efficiency. A lot of beautiful structured matrices have great asymptotic complexity but terrible constants on a GPU, because GPUs are optimized for dense matrix multiplies. So you can have something that's n log n on paper and it's slower than a dense matmul for any n you actually care about. That was a real lesson, and it's a lot of why the Mamba work ended up being as much about the implementation, the hardware-aware scan, as about the math. If the structure doesn't map to something the hardware can execute well, you don't actually get the win.

And then the last dimension is sort of the modeling and optimization side, which is subtler. Structured matrices can be harder to train. When you parameterize a matrix in a constrained way, the loss landscape changes, things can be ill-conditioned, you have to think about initialization carefully. So even if the structure is expressive enough in principle, you might not be able to find the good solutions with gradient descent. Again, that's something we hit very directly with the state space work, where the parameterization mattered enormously for whether it trained at all.

So I guess if I had to summarize, I'd say the trade-off is real, but it's not one-dimensional. You're balancing expressivity, theoretical compute, actual hardware efficiency, and trainability, and the structures that have really worked are the ones where you get all four to line up, usually because the structure reflects something true about the domain. And I think there's a lot more room there. We've mostly explored a pretty small corner of the space of structured matrices, and I suspect there are structures for things like long context or multimodal data that we haven't found yet.

r001.rationale: The response says structured matrices constrain the function class and may give up expressivity compared with a dense matrix, which it describes as the most general form.

r002.rationale: It explains that structure acts as an inductive bias and can be chosen to match the problem, using convolution as an example.

r003.rationale: It states that structured matrices can have faster multiplication algorithms, including costs of n log n or linear instead of quadratic for dense matrices.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency. If you have a dense matrix, you can learn every entry independently, so you have a lot of flexibility. When you impose structure, you restrict the transformations that matrix can represent, but you can potentially make the computation much faster and use fewer parameters.

The question is whether you're giving up flexibility that actually matters for the task. Structure can also be a useful inductive bias: if it matches the problem, it can make learning easier. So the goal isn't necessarily to find the most expressive matrix or the fastest matrix in isolation. It's to find structure that preserves the capabilities you need while making the model practical to train and run.

r001.rationale: It says structure restricts the transformations a matrix can represent compared with a dense matrix, which has more flexibility.

r002.rationale: It describes structure as a useful inductive bias when it matches the problem.

r003.rationale: It says imposing structure can make computation much faster than using a dense matrix.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic trade-off is between expressivity and computational efficiency. If you use a completely general matrix, you have a lot of flexibility, but storing it and multiplying by it can be expensive. If you impose structure, you can often make those operations much faster and use fewer parameters, but you’re restricting what the matrix can represent.

The interesting question is whether that restriction is actually a good inductive bias for the problem. If you pick the right structure, you might preserve the behavior you care about while getting a much more efficient model. So I wouldn’t think of structure as necessarily sacrificing performance. It’s about finding a parameterization that gives you both useful modeling capacity and an efficient algorithm.

r001.rationale: It says a general matrix has more flexibility and imposing structure restricts what the matrix can represent.

r002.rationale: It says choosing the right structure can provide a useful inductive bias for the problem.

r003.rationale: It states that imposing structure can make matrix operations, including multiplication, much faster than using a general matrix.
